newsitem.title: USA: Clinton raises $650,000 for Democratic coffers.
newsitem.headline: Clinton raises $650,000 for Democratic coffers.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday helped collect another $650,000 for Democratic Party coffers, a day after denying he was a hypocrite for pushing campaign finance reform while continuing to raise money.

Clinton told 50 guests at a fund-raising dinner hosted by the Democratic Business Council that he was committed to winning congressional approval for a bill that would curb unlimited contributions to political parties.

"It will put more pressure on both Democrats and Republicans to go out and get more people to contribute and make more people feel like part of the system, and that will be a very good thing," Clinton told the guests, who paid $10,000 per person to hear the president and dine on gazpacho, swordfish, carrots and zucchini.

Corporations and political action committees were asked to donate $15,000 to attend the function, which raised $350,000 to help the debt-ridden Democratic Party reload for 1998 midterm congressional races.
Clinton has been speaking at DNC functions around the country this year, helping the party raise $19 million in the first half of 1997 alone, a White House spokesman said.

He also spoke to 35 guests at a Democratic National Committee dinner that raised $300,000, saying he hoped to win fast-track authority from Congress this year to negotiate the expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement.
Both dinners took place at the Mayflower Hotel.

In its Friday editions, the Washington Post said that among 4,000 documents delivered Monday to the Senate panel investigating fund-raising abuses were 12 call sheets prepared for Hillary Rodham Clinton asking her to call donors such as designer Ralph Lauren and ask for $100,000 or $50,000.
"Mrs. Clinton does not recall actually making any fund-raising calls, but she does not rule it out," the Post quoted the first lady's spokeswoman, Marsha Berry, as saying.
There were no notations under the heading "call results" on the 12 call sheets addressed to the first lady, it said.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee has begun an investigation to determine whether the DNC obstructed its inquiry by delaying delivery of the documents, which should have been turned over three months ago.

In his dinner address, Clinton also said he and Hillary planned a conference on affordable child care in late October, saying he was "obsessed" with finding ways to help parents juggle the dual challenge of working and raising children.

"I am still, I think obsessed is not too strong a word, with the challenge so many Americans face in succeeding in raising their children and succeeding at work, and there's still not a systematic network of child care out there," he said.
The president on Wednesday passionately refused to cut back on raising money for Democrats in the face of investigations into last year's campaign financing.

At a news conference, Clinton said he continued to solicit the kind of large, unregulated "soft money" contributions to political parties that he himself has proposed banning because he did not believe in "unilateral disarmament."
He complained that opposition Republicans still raised and spent twice as much money as Democrats.
